scenes.narration: One hundred and two point seven billion dollars. That is what Amazon spent on shipping in a single year, twenty twenty-five. More than the entire economy of many countries produces.

Now compare it with what Amazon earned from all its subscriptions, Prime fees, music, audiobooks and more. forty-nine point six billion dollars. By our calculation, the shipping bill alone was about twice as big. And Amazon says it plans to keep offering those shipping deals indefinitely.
So how can a membership that seems to cost Amazon so much be one of the smartest deals in business?

By the end of this video, you will know the four parts of the Prime machine. The fee, the flywheel, the hidden profit engines, and the cancellation maze that cost Amazon two and a half billion dollars.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: It began in February two thousand and five. Amazon introduced its first ever membership program. For a flat fee of seventy-nine dollars a year, members got unlimited two-day shipping for free, with no minimum purchase. Jeff Bezos called it all-you-can-eat express shipping, and admitted it was expensive for the company in the short term.

The price crept up. By twenty fifteen, Amazon described Prime as a ninety-nine dollar annual program. In twenty eighteen, it went to one hundred and nineteen. In February twenty twenty-two, Amazon raised it again, to one hundred and thirty-nine dollars a year, or fourteen ninety-nine a month. That is still the price today.

And people kept joining. In twenty eighteen, Bezos wrote that Prime had passed one hundred million paid members. Three years later, he wrote that Amazon had more than two hundred million Prime members worldwide. That is the last official total the company has published.

All of Amazon's subscription fees together brought in about forty billion dollars in twenty twenty-three, forty-four billion in twenty twenty-four, and forty-nine point six billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. That line includes Prime, but also music, audiobooks, e-books and video. Amazon does not report Prime fees on their own. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six alone, subscriptions brought in about fourteen billion dollars, up about eleven percent on a year earlier, by our calculation.

Let me draw the deal. On one side, what a member pays, one hundred and thirty-nine dollars a year. On the other side, what the member gets, fast shipping, video, music and more. On paper, the member seems to get far more than they pay. In its accounts, Amazon describes Prime as an evolving suite of benefits, a single promise that it stands ready to deliver all year, and it spreads the fee over the months of the membership. So where does Amazon win?

scenes.narration: The answer starts with a single word that Amazon uses in its own annual report. Marketing.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In its annual report, Amazon writes that Prime and its other shipping offers are not counted in marketing expense. But the company says it views them as effective worldwide marketing tools, and intends to continue offering them indefinitely.

And those tools are expensive. Shipping costs rose from about eighty-nine billion dollars in twenty twenty-three to one hundred and two point seven billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. Fulfillment, the warehouses, staff and customer service, cost another one hundred and nine billion dollars. These numbers cover all of Amazon's customers, not just Prime members. But Prime is a big reason people order so often. And Amazon itself expects its cost of shipping to keep increasing, as customers use its shipping offers more.

Then there is entertainment. Amazon spent twenty-two point four billion dollars on video and music in twenty twenty-five, including the shows and movies offered with Prime. Content that keeps members coming back, even when they are not shopping.

Why spend so much? Because members buy more, and they buy from Amazon first. In his twenty twenty letter, Bezos estimated that Prime created about six hundred and thirty dollars of value per member, by the company's own calculation. A member who has paid for free shipping has every reason to shop there again.

Let me draw the flywheel. Lower prices and fast delivery bring more customers. More customers bring more sellers. More sellers bring more choice, which brings more customers again. Prime sits at the center, turning a single fee into a habit.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: But the flywheel alone does not explain the profits. For that, you have to look at two businesses most shoppers never see.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The first is advertising. Every sponsored product you scroll past on Amazon is an ad that a seller paid for. Amazon's advertising revenue grew from about forty-seven billion dollars in twenty twenty-three to sixty-eight point six billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. By our calculation, that is a rise of almost half in two years.

And Prime itself became an ad channel. In early twenty twenty-four, Prime Video started showing ads to members by default. Watching without them cost an extra two dollars and ninety-nine cents a month. In twenty twenty-six, Amazon replaced that with a new ad-free tier, at four ninety-nine a month.

The second engine is Amazon Web Services, the cloud computing business that rents out servers to other companies. By our calculation, A W S brought in only eighteen percent of Amazon's sales in twenty twenty-five, but fifty-seven percent of its operating income. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, its share was about sixty-three percent.

The difference is in the margins. By our calculation, A W S kept about thirty-five cents of operating profit from every dollar of sales. The North American store kept about seven cents. The cloud pays for a large part of the empire. The store builds the habit.

Let me draw where Amazon's profit comes from. Here is the store, by far the biggest in sales, with a thin slice of profit. Here is advertising, growing fast on top of the store's traffic. And here is the cloud, smaller in sales but the biggest in profit. Prime feeds the first two.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Keeping members inside the machine matters so much that, according to regulators, Amazon made it hard to leave.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In June twenty twenty-three, the Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon. It alleged that the company had duped millions of consumers into enrolling in Prime without knowing it, using designs known as dark patterns.

Then there was the way out. According to the complaint, Amazon's internal name for the cancellation process was Iliad, after Homer's epic about the long, hard Trojan War. Cancelling meant a four-page, six-click, fifteen-option process. Joining took one or two clicks.

In September twenty twenty-five, Amazon settled. It agreed to pay a one billion dollar civil penalty and one point five billion dollars in refunds, for an estimated thirty-five million consumers. Amazon recorded a two point five billion dollars charge in its third quarter results. The settlement also requires a clear way to decline Prime and a simple way to cancel it. These were the regulator's allegations, and the company did not admit wrongdoing.

Let me draw the two doors. The way in, one button, one click. The way out, a corridor of pages, choices and offers, each one asking if you are sure. When leaving is harder than joining, people stay, and every month they stay, the fee keeps arriving.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And every summer, Amazon turns that membership into one giant shopping event.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Prime Day is a sale only members can fully use. In twenty twenty-five, Amazon expanded it to four days and called it the biggest Prime Day event ever. It is so important to the business that when it moved from the third quarter to the second in twenty twenty-six, Amazon had to explain the shift to investors.

That is the real trick. Prime turns a store into a club. You pay first, then you shop. The fee is small compared to Amazon's costs. But it changes behavior, it brings members back to the app before any other store, and every visit feeds the advertising machine.

Let me put the whole machine together. A fee that locks in the habit. Shipping and video that make the fee feel like a bargain. Advertising that profits from all that traffic. A cloud business that throws off cash. And an exit door that was, according to regulators, deliberately hard to find.

So what is the hidden economics of Amazon Prime? Prime is not a product that has to make money on its own. It is the glue. It keeps hundreds of millions of people shopping, watching and clicking in one place. Amazon may spend more on delivery than Prime fees bring in. But what it buys with that money is something far more valuable. Your habit.
